Chapter 3: Expressing Love in Friendships and Family Relationships
Once you’ve built that solid foundation of self-awareness, it’s only natural to start focusing outward—toward all the relationships that fill your everyday life.
For single adults, friendships and family ties are often the heart of emotional support and connection. But let’s be real—these relationships can be just as complicated as any romantic partnership, especially when it comes to showing and receiving love.
Friendships, in particular, give us a special place to practice our love languages. Unlike family, where connections are shaped by history or obligation, friendships are chosen. They’re kept alive by mutual effort. That makes them the perfect space to experiment with new ways of showing appreciation and care.
Picture your own group of friends for a moment. Maybe one person lights up when you remember their birthday or bring them a thoughtful gift. Someone else might feel closest to you during deep conversations or while you’re out on some wild adventure together. If everyone just sticks to their own favorite ways of showing affection, someone’s bound to feel left out. But when friends take time to learn each other’s love languages, something shifts. Suddenly, a simple handwritten note, a spontaneous road trip, or even helping out with a small favor can mean the world—because it matches what the other person values most.
Family relationships can really benefit from this kind of thoughtfulness, too. Siblings, parents, even those cousins you only see at holidays—they all come with their own patterns, shaped by years of shared memories. These patterns can be comforting, but sometimes, they’re a source of frustration, especially if our emotional needs don’t quite line up.
Think about a parent who shows love by cooking dinner or fixing things around the house. They might not realize their child is really craving a heartfelt compliment or one-on-one time. By bringing the idea of love languages into these conversations, families can start to bridge those gaps—and maybe even heal some old wounds along the way.
So, how can you put this into practice with friends and family? Here are a few ideas:
Words of Affirmation—try giving a genuine compliment, saying thank you, or acknowledging someone’s achievements, whether you’re chatting or leaving a note.
Quality Time—make plans for regular get-togethers, jump into a shared hobby, or just be present with someone—phones down, distractions off.
Receiving Gifts—give small, meaningful tokens that show you’re really tuned in to what the other person likes or needs.
Acts of Service—help out with chores, run an errand, or offer support when things get tough.
Physical Touch—for the people who are comfortable with it, a hug, a high-five, or a reassuring hand on the shoulder can make a big difference.
Of course, not every way of expressing love fits every relationship. It’s so important to respect cultural norms, personal boundaries, and what each person feels comfortable with. The real goal here isn’t to force any one style—it’s about finding honest, heartfelt ways to show you care.
And when misunderstandings pop up—as they always do—it helps to circle back to the love languages. Most conflicts come from mismatched expectations or needs that haven’t been spoken out loud. If you can approach these moments with curiosity and empathy, you’ll move past the surface stuff and get to what really matters underneath.
So here’s the key takeaway: expressing love languages in friendships and family is all about intentionality. It’s a choice to truly see and value each person as they are, and to create spaces where everyone feels known and cherished.
